title: He Helped Wreck the Academy's Idea of Art, Then Spent Thirty Years Painting Like Renoir
standfirst: In February 1908 William Glackens helped organise the exhibition that got his circle nicknamed the Ashcan School. The same year, a Durand-Ruel retrospective of forty-one Renoir canvases quietly pulled him the opposite way. This undated, untraceable Washington Square scene sits inside that argument — and the corpus's flat label for it, Impressionism, turns out to be earned rather than assumed.

sections.heading: No Museum Has It, No Sale Record Exists, and the Date Is a Guess
sections.body: Search for this canvas today and almost every result is the same kind of site: a print-on-demand shop offering a framed reproduction, a stock-image reseller, a gallery that will giclée it to whatever size fits a wall. No museum's online catalogue lists it. No auction house has a public sale record for it. The corpus gives no year for it, and nothing I could actually read pinned one down — only a repeated "circa 1911" trailing across the reproduction sites, none of which cite where the date comes from. That is an odd fate for a painter whose other Washington Square scenes are catalogued, credited and exhibited. It suggests this particular picture has spent most of its life in private hands, unremarked on, while the argument over what kind of painter made it was happening somewhere else entirely — starting with an exhibition Glackens helped organise against nearly everything decorative in American painting.

sections.heading: The Exhibition That Got Them Called Ashcans
sections.body: In February 1908 eight painters who had been shut out of the National Academy of Design's official shows opened their own exhibition at the Macbeth Galleries in New York. Robert Henri led it; the group's five realists — Glackens, John Sloan, George Luks and Everett Shinn among them — painted saloons, tenements, streetcars and prizefights, the subjects the Academy's own salons wouldn't hang, while Arthur B. Davies, Ernest Lawson and Maurice Prendergast worked in entirely different directions under the same banner. Reviews split: some called it daring, more called it dreary and badly drawn. Even inside that room, Glackens was already the outlier. He had made his name in 1901 with a scene of Hammerstein's Roof Garden, and by 1908 he was still the one in the group reaching for leisure — restaurants, parks, roof gardens — in a palette noticeably brighter than Sloan's or Luks's. The revolt he helped start was against the Academy's taste. It was never quite a revolt against beauty.

sections.heading: Forty-One Renoirs, Same Year, Across Town
sections.body: The same year, Durand-Ruel's New York gallery mounted a retrospective of forty-one paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir — a scale of exposure to his work Glackens hadn't had before. According to the museums that later paired the two artists in a comparative exhibition, Glackens's absorption of Renoir barely registered in his own painting before that 1908 show; afterward, it reshaped it. The change wasn't sudden — Glackens kept exhibiting with Henri's circle for years yet — but the direction was set: looser, sweeter brushwork, warmer flesh tones, subjects drawn from pleasure rather than the street's harder edges. By the time critics started calling him "the American Renoir," it read less like an insult than a description of a debt he had never tried to hide. Asked about the comparison, his answer was blunt: ["Can you think of a better man to follow than Renoir?"](https://www.huntermuseum.org/exhibition/william-j-glackens-and-pierre-auguste-renoir-affinities-and-distinctions)

sections.heading: Twenty Years Painting the Same Few Hundred Feet
sections.body: Glackens had studios on the south side of Washington Square from soon after he arrived in New York in 1896, and from 1910 he owned the townhouse at 10 West 9th Street outright, adding a mansard roof that gave its top floor seventeen-foot ceilings and the light he wanted to paint by. Between 1908 and 1914 he painted the square in front of it more than twenty times — nannies and children on the paths, the arch in different weather, an Italian-American parade crossing the grass with its flags out in 1912, a bus disgorging passengers in 1910. The subjects barely varied; the handling did, growing looser and brighter across those six years in exactly the direction the 1908 Renoir show had pointed him. Today's picture, of one specific address on that same square, belongs somewhere inside that run — a single canvas from a painter working out, in public and over and over, what kind of painting he now wanted to make.

sections.heading: Barnes Hands Him $20,000 and an Open Brief
sections.body: In 1912 Glackens's old Central High School classmate Albert C. Barnes, by then rich and buying art on a scale most dealers had never seen, sent him to Paris with $20,000 and an open brief to buy whatever he thought mattered. Glackens delivered: by early March he had assembled roughly twenty paintings, including his first Cézanne, his first Picasso, his first Van Gogh, and a Renoir bought for 7,000 francs. The shipment reached Philadelphia on 2 April 1912 and became the seed of what is now the Barnes Foundation's collection. Glackens wasn't uncritical of what he saw in Paris — he warned Barnes that art was ["in a strange state at present among the youth"](https://blog.phillyhistory.org/index.php/2012/04/april-2-1912-barnes-unpacks-his-first-shipment-of-french-art/) — but the trip put him in sustained, close contact with exactly the paintings his own work had been moving toward since that Durand-Ruel show four years earlier.

sections.heading: The Charge of Imitation, and the Answer He Kept Giving
sections.body: None of it went unchallenged. By the 1920s and 1930s, critics who had once welcomed Glackens as an Ashcan realist were writing him off as derivative, his artistic personality, in one description, "blunted by too close an imitation of Renoir's late style." Glackens kept painting the way he wanted regardless, and died suddenly in 1938 while on holiday in Connecticut; the Whitney's memorial show that year ran to 132 works and was well received, decades after the critics who mattered most to him in 1908 had already made up their minds. The corpus's one-word label on today's picture, Impressionism, is therefore not really a mislabelling, the way it can be for painters only loosely associated with a movement — it is closer to a verdict Glackens earned the hard way, through a fight that started with an exhibition against nearly everything decorative and ended with him defending, in print, his devotion to the most decorative painter of his generation.
